summary.text: Olga is remembered as a ruler of Kiev, grandmother of Vladimir, and Equal-to-the-Apostles. The published life places her conversion within the political and religious history of Rus and its relationship with Constantinople. It draws on chronicle traditions as well as liturgical remembrance. Those sources and their commemorative interpretation are not presented as interchangeable with contemporary documentary records.

blocks.text: OLGA, wife of Igor, prince of Kiev, and afterwards (from 945) regent for Sviatoslav her son, was baptized at Constantinople about 955 and died about 969. She was afterwards canonized in the Russian church, and is now commemorated on the 11th of July.

blocks.text: Before her conversion, the chronicle portrays a ruler who took violent revenge on the Drevlyani. She reorganized tribute collection and administration, later received baptism with the name Helen, and maintained Christian worship despite her son’s refusal to convert. The dates and number of her journeys to Constantinople are disputed in the sources discussed by the published life.

blocks.text: The Greek Archdiocese preserves the well-known chronicle-style story in which the emperor asks Olga to marry him. She first asks him to be her baptismal sponsor, then points out that marriage would violate the new spiritual relationship. This is a transmitted narrative about her wisdom; it is not evidence that every detail can be independently dated or verified. The account ends with her return carrying clergy, sacred texts, and icons, while her son remains pagan.
